# The Weight of Ordinary Things

There's a coffee cup on my desk with a chip on the rim that I keep meaning to replace but never do. It's the kind of small imperfection that nobody else would notice, but I feel it every morning against my lip, a tiny rough edge that's become familiar enough to be almost comforting. This is what I've been thinking about lately—how we live with broken things, how we accommodate ourselves to imperfection until it becomes the shape of our days.

I used to believe that getting older meant accumulating wisdom, like adding rooms to a house. I imagined I would eventually have answers, or at least fewer questions. Instead, what I've noticed is the opposite. Each year seems to ask something new that I'm unprepared for, and I find myself saying "I don't know" more often than I ever did at twenty. There's something unexpectedly liberating about this, though also disorienting.

Last week, I watched a bird—I think it was a sparrow, though I'm not certain because I don't know birds the way I should—attempt to build a nest in a peculiar spot near my window. It kept dropping twigs. Over and over, the bird would arrange them carefully, and they would fall. I watched this for maybe twenty minutes, and I thought about failure, about whether the bird was frustrated or whether it simply continued operating from instinct, following the program of nest-building without any emotional weight attached to the repeated failures. How much easier that would be.

But we're not like that, are we? We carry our failures. We build narratives around them. We wake up at 3 AM thinking about conversations from years ago, replaying moments where we said the wrong thing or didn't say anything at all. I've made a kind of peace with this—not acceptance exactly, but an acknowledgment that this might be the price of being conscious. The bird doesn't lie awake wondering if its nest-building efforts were meaningful. I do, sometimes, about much less important things.

What strikes me most about being alive now is how much beauty exists alongside suffering without either one diminishing the other. I can be genuinely moved by a sunset and simultaneously aware of terrible things happening in the world. A friend can tell me about heartbreak one moment, and we can laugh at something ridiculous the next, and both of those emotional states feel true and real. I used to think these contradictions meant something was wrong with me, that I wasn't responding appropriately to events. Now I think this is just what it means to be human—to be capacious enough to hold multiple truths simultaneously.

I've been rereading some of my favorite books lately, the ones I read when I was younger. It's strange to encounter your former self through the margins you've annotated, the passages you underlined. Often, I disagree with what that younger version found important. Sometimes I'm moved by her passion, her certainty about things. Other times I cringe at her interpretations. But mostly I'm struck by how the act of reading itself is different now. I'm slower. I linger. I reread sentences not because I don't understand them, but because I want to sit with them awhile.

There's a specific kind of exhaustion I experience now that I don't remember from before. It's not just physical tiredness, though there's plenty of that. It's more like I'm tired from the effort of maintaining all the versions of myself that different situations require. With my family, I'm one person. At work, another. With old friends, I become some previous iteration. With new friends, I'm still figuring out who I am. Each of these is authentic, and yet the switching between them, the constant calibration—it takes something out of me. I wonder if this is something everyone feels, or if some people have achieved an integration I haven't managed yet.

I've started noticing how many of our daily conversations are performative. We ask "How are you?" not because we want an honest answer, but because it's the script. When people ask me, I almost always say "fine," even when I'm not fine at all. Sometimes I want to tell the truth, to say, "Actually, I've been having a lot of difficult thoughts lately," but there's no mechanism for that in casual conversation. The form doesn't allow for content. This isn't anyone's fault, exactly. It's the price of navigating a world with other people efficiently. But I do wonder what would happen if we all started answering honestly.

The older I get, the less I understand children. Not individual children—children I know are fascinating and their interior lives sometimes seem less opaque to me than adults. But children in general, as a phenomenon. Where does the randomness come from? How are they formed? The mystery of it is greater now than when I was younger and had confident theories about child development and what I would do differently if I had kids. Now I just think: that's a tiny person, and nobody really knows what they're thinking, and they might become anyone.

I think about legacy sometimes, though that word has begun to feel grandiose. What does any of us leave behind? I don't mean in the sense of monuments or achievements, though some people have those. I mean the smaller legacies—the way we treated someone, a conversation someone still remembers, the way we influenced how someone else moves through the world. My grandmother has been dead for seven years, and I still catch myself about to tell her something I saw, forgetting she's gone. But also, I hear her phrases in my head. Her particular way of looking at things lives in me. Maybe that's legacy—not permanence, but a kind of ongoing influence.

I'm running out of words now, and I feel like I haven't reached any conclusions, haven't tied this up neatly. But perhaps that's appropriate. Life doesn't come to conclusions very often. We're mostly in the middle of things, the ongoing and untidy middle where we're trying to figure things out with incomplete information and competing desires and the knowledge that we're running out of time without knowing how much time we have.

The chip on my coffee cup is still there. The bird probably finished its nest, or abandoned it and started again somewhere else. The world continues with its specific combination of beauty and difficulty, and I continue through it, carrying questions, offering imperfect responses, hoping it's enough.
